_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Mishna. He gives five sela: since one of them is a firstborn.
rashi:a1.2: The father is exempt: since he can say, “The firstborn is the one who died.” The same applies to the remaining son: he too is exempt. The mishna words it “the father is exempt” because of the next clause, which goes on to teach “If the father died…”
gershom:a1.1: If one of them died within thirty days, the father is exempt: since he can say, “The firstborn is the one who died.”
rashi:a2.2: The obligation took effect: the father’s property became obligated to the priest, as to a creditor, and the two of them together must pay.
rashi:a2.3: The priest has nothing here: since [the father] says to him, “The female came out first,” and the priest has the weaker hand, for the burden of proof rests on the one who would take from his fellow.
gershom:a2.1: But if not, they are exempt: since each one of them can put him off.
gershom:a3.1: Rabbi Yehuda says: the obligation took effect on the property, and they cannot put him off.
gershom:a4.1: [On the mishna of 48b, two priests:] He cannot take it back from them: since each [priest] can say, “What I hold is the redemption of the living one.”
gershom:a5.1: [On the mishna of 48b:] A male and a female: where one [wife] bore a male and the other a female; or two males and a female, where one bore a male and a female and the other a male: he gives five sela to the priest on account of the one who bore a male alone. [A phrase repeated in the printed text is left out.]
gershom:a6.1: [On the mishna of 48b:] Two females and a male: where one bore a male and a female and the other a female; or [two males and two females, where] each bore a male and a female: the priest has nothing here.
gershom:a7.1: [On the mishna of 48b, apparently the case of one wife who had given birth before and one who had not:] And they bore two males, and they were intermingled: the father is exempt, since the burden of proof rests on the one who would take from his fellow.
gershom:a8.1: A creditor who holds a document against [a] Yosef ben Shimon collects it from them, since he says to him: “If it is yours…” and so on.
gershom:a9.1: And this property too, while they have not divided it, is held in partnership. [Rava:] It is a guarantor for him, so that the creditor collects from it. Is there anything where one cannot claim from the man himself — for [the father] died within thirty days, when he was not yet obligated in the redemption — and yet one can claim from his property, which is a guarantor? [The printed text puts the word “not” here in parentheses, marking it as a word to delete.] But we learned: “One who lends…”, and we hold that one does not claim from the guarantor first, only from the debtor; and here one cannot claim from the debtor.
gershom:a10.1: And where there is a lot of property for each one: so too he takes it, even though they divided.
gershom:a11.1: Half heirs and half purchasers: for each one conveyed his share to the other in return for what he takes.
gershom:a12.1: A loan written in the Torah: such as the five sela of a firstborn.
rashi:a3.1: Gemara. But the property is on lien: since it is a full debt.
rashi:a4.1: And he puts him off: and says, “I am not the firstborn; my brother is.”
rashi:a4.2: Even when they did not divide, and so on: one cannot say that [the priest] seizes the property on account of their father, since the father was obligated in nothing; it is only on account of the sons that he would seize it. So why does the mishna teach “If they gave [before they divided]…”, which implies that if they have not divided, they are obligated?
rashi:a5.1: Two Yosef ben Shimons: a man produced a promissory note against one of them, and each put him off, saying, “It is not me but my fellow.” The two of them bought one field together: the creditor seizes half of it, since he says to him, and so on. Here too the priest seizes five sela from the property, which they hold together, and he likewise says to them: “If you are the firstborn, I take from your share, and if your brother is the firstborn, I take from his share; and between the two of you, settle it.”
rashi:a6.1: Whom he cannot claim from directly: since each one of them puts him off.
rashi:a6.2: He shall not claim payment; and we hold: what does “he shall not claim payment” mean? That he may not claim from the guarantor first, until he has claimed from the borrower and the borrower has nothing to pay with.
rashi:a7.1: So too he takes: even if they divided, since the property became on lien during the father’s lifetime; and although it is an oral loan, it is collected from the heirs if the inheritance is as large as the debt.
rashi:a8.1: Of Rav Asi: as found in Bava Kamma, chapter one (9a).
rashi:a8.2: Half heirs and half purchasers: since he is unsure whether there is retroactive clarification [bereira], in which case they are heirs, or there is no retroactive clarification, in which case they are purchasers; therefore they are half heirs and half purchasers.
rashi:a8.3: A loan written in the Torah: such as the five sela of the redemption of a son, which the Merciful One awarded to the priest.
tosafot:a3.1: But the property is on lien to them: [the questioner] now holds that brothers who divided are heirs, and an oral loan is collected from heirs; or alternatively he holds that a loan written in the Torah is like one written in a document. But in the conclusion [the Gemara] says that this is exactly what they disagree about.
tosafot:a8.1: And everyone accepts the opinion of Rav Asi, and so on: this implies that Rabbi Meir is unsure whether there is retroactive clarification [bereira] or not, like Rav Asi. This is puzzling, since Rabbi Meir does not accept bereira in the case of one who buys wine from Samaritans, [cited] in chapter Merubba (Bava Kamma 69b) and in chapter Kol HaGet (Gittin 25a). And it is puzzling about Rava himself, who here sets them both as following Rav Asi, since in chapter Kol HaGet (Gittin 26a) [it is stated] that both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon accept bereira. One may distinguish: there is bereira where one stipulates explicitly, for example “the two log that I will separate in the future”, “I am having relations with you on condition that father consents”, and “this is your bill of divorce if I die”. This also resolves the contradiction between one statement of Shmuel and another: he does not accept bereira at the end of Beitza (37b), regarding two who bought an animal in partnership; yet in chapter Mi SheAḥazo (Gittin 75b), where Shmuel instituted [a condition] for the bill of divorce of a dangerously ill man, he accepts bereira, and it is a bill of divorce [effective] from when he dies, as is deduced at the beginning of Kol HaGet.
tosafot:a8.2: In brief: Rav Asi’s statement is found in Bava Kamma chapter one (9a) and in Bava Batra (107a). There Rav and Shmuel disagree about brothers who divided, after which a creditor seized one brother’s share: Rav says the division is void, since they are heirs; Shmuel says that brother has lost out, since they are purchasers without a guarantee; and Rav Asi is unsure. Tosafot weighs two explanations of Rav Asi. First: of the remaining property he takes a quarter in land and a quarter in money, since it is unclear whether he is like an heir (who takes it all in land) or like a purchaser with a guarantee (who can be paid off in money); on this explanation Rabbeinu Ḥananel’s reading “three brothers” (Bava Batra 107a) cannot stand. Second: he takes half of his proper share, a quarter in land and a quarter in money, and loses the other half. Tosafot objects to the second: if the only doubt were heir versus purchaser without a guarantee, he would take his [half] share in land; should the added doubt that he might be a purchaser with a guarantee weaken him? On the contrary, he should take half his share in land and the quarter in money. Further, our daf sets the mishna where there are only five sela; if Rav Asi counted them heirs for only a quarter, they would be exempt even with ten sela, since the priest could collect only the quarter in which they are heirs, which is half of five. Rashi’s first explanation in Bava Kamma (9a), that he takes half his share, in land or in money, fits either reading. Yet one may ask how the Talmud knows that Rav Asi doubts whether they are heirs at all; perhaps he only doubts whether they are purchasers with or without a guarantee. And “a quarter” would not be stated twice, since it is taught as “either… or”. The last explanation seems right, and the reading “three brothers” should be rejected altogether: the Talmud’s way is to speak of five (five claimants, five women whose offspring were intermingled), not three, since two are the same as three. If you ask: since Rav Asi is unsure whether they are heirs or purchasers, why not rule that the burden of proof rests on the one who would take from his fellow? Even Sumakhos would not divide here, for this is a doubt of the Sages about the ruling. Answer: there are matters where, when the law is in doubt for the Sages, they treat it as certainly half one way and half the other, as in Bava Metzia 83a (porters who must pay half, as close to negligence and close to accident), Bava Batra 145a (Rabbi Yosei: he betrothed with twenty and is repaid thirty halves), Bava Batra 126a (the firstborn and a loan owed to the estate), and Bava Metzia 102a (the bathhouse, where they divide the intercalated month according to everyone, without needing Sumakhos). There are also matters where, since no halakha was stated, whoever acts like either master has acted properly; and matters left to the judges’ discretion, as in Bava Batra 62b. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a8.3: In brief: And everyone agrees that a loan written in the Torah is not like one written in a document: this holds in the conclusion too, which says they disagree about Rav Asi or about Rav Pappa; that implies that if both accepted Rav Asi and Rav Pappa, they would be exempt because of “five, not half of five”. This is puzzling, since below in this chapter (49b) it says that Rabbi Yehuda holds a loan written in the Torah is like one written in a document. A further difficulty: on the conclusion that they disagree about Rav Pappa, Rabbi Yehuda rejects Rav Pappa and holds that an oral loan is collected even from purchasers. Does Rabbi Yehuda reject the mishna in Get Pashut (Bava Batra 175a), “One who lends with a document collects from mortgaged property; orally, from unencumbered property”? Moreover, Rav Pappa’s main point was not that, but that an oral loan is collected from heirs, against Rav and Shmuel, who say it is collected neither from heirs nor from purchasers; that it is not collected from purchasers is no novelty, being plain throughout the Talmud. Tosafot explains: according to the conclusion, it is not exactly Rav Pappa that is meant, but [a debt] like an oral loan, such as this redemption of a son, though it is written [in the Torah]. In Kiddushin chapter one (29b) the passage below is found, and there the reading is “Rabbi Yehuda follows his own reasoning, for he says a loan written in the Torah is like one written in a document”, which fits the reasoning here. Alternatively, they do disagree about Rav Pappa himself, and Rav Pappa must be speaking of a loan written in the Torah: in Kiddushin chapter one (13b) Rav Pappa says the halakha is that an oral loan is collected from heirs, since the lien is by Torah law, while in Get Pashut (Bava Batra 176a) the reason given is “so as not to lock the door before borrowers”. So Kiddushin must be speaking of a loan written in the Torah, holding that it is collected from heirs but not from purchasers; and that is the ruling Rabbi Yehuda rejects here, holding that it is collected even from purchasers. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a8.4: A loan written in the Torah: this means specifically such things as the redemption of a son, valuations, damages and the like, which one would not owe had the Torah not obligated him. But an ordinary oral loan, even though it is written “the man to whom you lend shall bring the pledge out to you” (Deuteronomy 24:11), and even though that verse speaks of an oral loan, does not count as “written” so as to be like one written in a document, since the Torah did not create the obligation by writing it; even without the verse it is obvious that he must repay what he was lent.
rashi:b2.1: And not half of five: therefore they are exempt. Since they divided, they are half purchasers, and only two and a half sela remain as inheritance; and from the purchasers’ half he takes nothing, since an oral loan is not collected from purchasers.
rashi:b2.2: And even half of five: and he takes the half that is inheritance.
rashi:b3.1: If so: that according to Rabbi Yehuda he takes only half, [can he say] “the obligation took effect on the property”? [A rhetorical question.]
rashi:b3.2: We read “he should have said, the man is obligated”, and we do not read “became obligated”. That is: Rabbi Yehuda should have taught “they are obligated”, meaning they are not entirely exempt, as we said, but are at least obligated for half of five. It does not fit to teach “the property became obligated”, since [on this reading] he died after thirty days; rather, because of the division they made, by which they became purchasers, the priest has lost, according to Rabbi Yehuda himself, half of what the property had been obligated for.
rashi:b3.3: Brothers who divided: and each of the two may be the firstborn.
rashi:b3.4: Ten dinars for this one and ten dinars for that one: which is two and a half sela.
rashi:b4.1: If we say, both the inheritance share and the purchase share: and when it teaches “they are obligated”, it means for half of five, since you said that everyone accepts Rav Asi and Rav Pappa; and we learn from it [that Rabbi Yehuda holds] five, and even half of five.
rashi:b4.2: Even fewer than ten: say eight, where only two sela reach the priest; he should take them, for once the priest takes less than five, he takes whatever comes his way; “half of five” equally includes a third of five. So why does it teach “and if not, they are exempt”?
rashi:b5.1: Rather, it is obvious: ten dinars of inheritance for each one, apart from the purchasers’ half, which makes five sela of inheritance.
rashi:b6.1: And here: in the mishna, they disagree about Rav Asi or about Rav Pappa. Rabbi Meir accepts both Rav Asi and Rav Pappa; since there are only five [sela] in all, [the priest] takes nothing, [for it is] five and not half of five. Rabbi Yehuda accepts Rav Asi, that half is purchase, but rejects Rav Pappa, holding that an oral loan is collected from purchasers, and so the priest takes all of it. Alternatively, he rejects Rav Asi, and all of it is inheritance, and the priest takes all of it. And now that this is his view, we read the baraita this way: if there are ten dinars for this one and ten dinars for that one, all together, they must give all the property; and if not, if there are not five [sela] in all, they are exempt, [for it is] five and not half of five.
rashi:b7.1: There are those who teach this entire discussion on the latter clause: of the mishna, the statement of Rabbi Yehuda.
rashi:b9.1: And one of them bought a field from the other: here too, since we hold that brothers who divided are purchasers, as there is no bereira, [this is the case] where Rabbi Yehuda obligates them.
rashi:b10.1: As in the first version: [ending with] “Rather, they disagree about Rav Asi and Rav Pappa.”
rashi:b11.1: Mishna. Two wives: of one man.
rashi:b11.2: And they gave birth to two males: out of sight, so that they were intermingled.
rashi:b11.3: If he gave to one priest: the father [gave] the redemption of both, [the priest] must return five sela to him, since [one child] died within thirty days and it became clear that it was a nonviable birth, and [the priest] took it without right.
rashi:b11.4: He cannot take it back from them: since each one puts him off and says, “I am holding them for the redemption of the living one.”
rashi:b12.1: Or two males and a female: his wives gave birth out of sight. He gives five sela to the priest, since either way one is a firstborn: if one wife bore two males, the first is a firstborn; and if one bore a male and a female, then her fellow bore a male alone, and he is a firstborn; and the one born with the female is exempt, since perhaps the female came out first, and the burden of proof rests on the one who would take from his fellow.
rashi:b12.2: The priest has nothing here: since one can say the females came out first, and there is no firstborn here.
rashi:b13.1: The father is exempt: since he can say, “The son of the one giving birth for the first time is the one who died.”
rashi:b14.1: If they gave before they divided, and so on: like the ruling of the case above, because of Rav Asi and Rav Pappa.
rashi:b14.2: A male and a female: one can say that the one who had not given birth bore the female, and there is no firstborn here.
rashi:b15.1: If one of them died: one of the newborns, [the priest] returns five sela to them, and the two fathers divide it.
rashi:b15.2: And they cannot take it back: since each [priest] says, “I am holding it for the living one; the one it was given to me for did not die”; and whoever would take from his fellow has the weaker hand.
rashi:b16.1: The fathers are exempt: since each one says to the priest, “The female is mine.”
rashi:b16.2: And the son is obligated to redeem himself: since in any case he is a firstborn.
rashi:b16.3: Two females and a male: one can say that one [woman] bore a female and the other a male and a female, and the female came out first. Therefore the priest has nothing here, since one can say the first-time mother bore the female. [Rashi’s comment] ends here. And the same applies to two males and two females.
rashi:b19.1: Gemara. With one priest too: who took from two fathers; when this father goes to him, let the priest put him off and say, “It is not yours that died but your fellow’s, and you are not the one I have a case with.”
tosafot:b2.1: For Rabbi Meir holds five: this is not like “five cattle” [Exodus 21:37], where we conclude (Bava Kamma 71b) that the Merciful One meant even five halves of cattle, because those are payments, and he must pay what he owes. Here, though, the Merciful One placed on him a mitzva of five sela, and it is not fulfilled with less than five. And although one may pay [the five sela] to ten priests one after another, that is not comparable here, since here he is liable for only half of five.
tosafot:b11.1: And if he gave to two priests, he cannot take it back from them: and if you say: since had he not given he would not be required to give, now that he has given, let it be like a case where a priest seized [gifts by force], where we take it away from him, as is said in chapter Shenayim Oḥazin (Bava Metzia 6b)? Here it is easier, since he does not know from whom to take it back. But below it is harder, regarding a child who died on the thirtieth day, where Rabbi Akiva says: if he gave, he shall not take it back, and if he did not give, he need not give. Since if he did not give he need not give, now too that he gave, let it be like a priest who seized! One may answer: since at the outset he gives it to him as a priestly gift, then even though it later became clear that, had the priest not taken it, it would not have been right to take it out of doubt, we do not say we take it away from him. So too the case of one who arrives in the middle of the month, at the end of [chapter] HaShoel (Bava Metzia 102b): even though at the start of the month it all belongs to the landlord, we do not compare it to a priest who seized.
tosafot:b14.1: If they gave before they divided, and so on: some explanation is needed of why it is necessary to teach the dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda in both [mishnayot].
gershom:b1.1: Rabbi Meir holds that it is five sela that one must give the priest, and not half of five; that is why Rabbi Meir says that if they divided they are exempt, since they are half purchasers and [that half] is not on lien to him.
gershom:b2.1: And Rabbi Yehuda, who says the obligation took effect on the property even when they divided, holds five and even half of five.
gershom:b3.1: If so: that it speaks of [a father who died] after thirty [days], he should have said “the man is obligated”.
gershom:b4.1: Ten dinars for this one and ten dinars for that one: that is, twenty dinars, which are five sela.
gershom:b5.1: If so, five and even half of five: and since he may give less than five, “half” is not meant exactly; rather, even less than half.
gershom:b6.1: If so: that [he holds] even half of five, why specifically ten dinars?
gershom:b7.1: Rather, it is obvious: ten dinars of inheritance for each, and the five sela are collected from them out of their inheritance; evidently Rabbi Yehuda holds five and not half of five.
gershom:b8.1: They disagree about Rav Asi and Rav Pappa. That is: if both of them accept Rav Pappa, they disagree about Rav Asi; and if they accept Rav Asi, who says brothers who divided are half heirs and half purchasers, they disagree about Rav Pappa. Rabbi Meir holds like Rav Pappa, that an oral loan is not collected from purchasers; that is why he says that if they divided they are exempt where there are only five sela, since the Merciful One said five, and not half of five. And Rabbi Yehuda rejects Rav Pappa, [holding that the money] is collected even from purchasers, since the property became obligated. And if both hold like Rav Pappa, that an oral loan is not collected from purchasers, they disagree about Rav Asi: Rabbi Yehuda does not hold like Rav Asi; rather, they are all heirs, and he can collect all five sela, since the property became obligated.
gershom:b9.1: And one of them bought a field from the other: this is like their having divided, since the other has no share in it, and the creditor collects from [the buyer], since he says to him, “If it is yours…” and so on. So too the priest says to each of these brothers: “If you are the firstborn, I take your portion; and if your brother is the firstborn, the property was on lien to me before you [acquired it].”
gershom:b10.1: Rava said: Now consider, and so on: and all the difficulties we raised in the first version, up to the last “If so”, and as we resolved it: rather, they disagree about Rav Asi and Rav Pappa.
gershom:b11.1: Two wives: of two men, who had not given birth, and they bore two males and they were intermingled: this one gives, and so on.
gershom:b12.1: They cannot take it back from him: since [the priests] can put them off, for each one says, “I am holding the redemption of the living one.”
gershom:b13.1: A male and a female, and they were intermingled: the fathers are exempt, since each can say, “The female is mine”; but the son is obligated to redeem himself.
gershom:b14.1: Two females and a male: where one bore a male and a female and one a female; or [two males and two females, where] each bore a male and a female.
gershom:b15.1: And they bore two males, and they were intermingled: this one whose wife had not given birth before, since she bore a male, even though one does not know which he is, gives five sela to the priest.
gershom:b16.1: They bore a male and a female, and they were intermingled: the priest has nothing here, since perhaps the one bearing her firstborn bore the female.
gershom:b17.1: What is different about two priests, that he cannot take it back from them, and what is different about one priest, that he returns it? With one priest too, he can put off each one, for he can say to each one, “What I hold is yours [the redemption of your living son].”
gershom:b18.1: Shmuel said: where each comes with authorization [from the other] and says to him, “If the one who died is mine, give it back to me; and if it is my fellow’s, here, I hold his authorization.” But with two priests they cannot make use of authorization, since each [priest] says, “I have only five sela, those of the living one.”
